source.title: Algorithmic Information Dynamics of Learning: A Certified, Differentiable Complexity Controller for Grokking
source.authors: Luan Ozelim; Abicumaran Uthamacumaran; H. Zenil

record.tranche_reason: Tests grokking timing and progress signals with a complexity-based controller and additional measurements; it is not an explicit replication of the original training recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own modular-arithmetic grokking runs, timing sweeps, complexity measurements, and weight-norm interventions. Related findings attributed to cited work are not recorded as rows. Some per-fraction timing results are shown only in figures; only trends explicitly described in the text are recorded.
record.test_reason: Mostly a controller paper, but its plain-training baselines and diagnostics bear on several versions. They show delayed generalization on modular arithmetic and a data-size trend (V1). They time candidate progress signals against the grok step (V2). They test weight-norm projection as a switch (V3). They show that weight-decay strength gates grokking and that removing decay causes relapse (V5). The kick-versus-plain comparisons measure the authors' own method and do not bear on any version.
record.recipe_differences: Uses small modular-arithmetic models but adds a differentiable function-map complexity controller and transient kicks; also evaluates parity, a transformer, and weight-norm interventions. The paper does not claim an explicit reproduction of the original training procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with task and training fraction (addition versus multiplication), norm radius and weight-decay regime, model architecture (MLP versus transformer), and whether an objective-shaping constraint is released. The authors also report that full-batch optimizer trajectories can shift by O(10^3) steps under float-level code-path reordering.
record.code_released: not stated (repository URL and final DOI are to be disclosed)
record.problems: Most original experiments use only 1–12 seeds per condition, and many timing means are conditional on successful grokking. Some data-fraction curves are figure-only. The study tests small tasks and maps, not large-scale models; the authors also note sensitivity of individual full-batch trajectories to float-level code-path changes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results were omitted. Rows R26–R29 record the multiplication complexity-boundary sweep as findings outside the listed version claims, rather than treating it as evidence for the low-norm efficiency account.

untested.parts: No Fourier or other circuit is identified, and the removal of memorizing components is not measured. Only timing of function-level complexity and geometric signals is tested.

Non-algorithmic data (images, text, molecules), initialization-scale changes and the lazy-to-rich transition are not tested. Sparse parity is still algorithmic. Norm is varied only by in-training projection.
Entire version; no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.

No circuit-efficiency comparison. No critical dataset size, and no ungrokking below it, tied to weight decay. The data threshold studied (Occam boundary) concerns complexity-kick recovery, not a weight-decay efficiency mechanism.
Entire version; learned algorithms are not compared across runs.
Entire version. Float-level code-path sensitivity is noted (O(10^3) steps) but not tested as a cause of the delay.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report a full exact per-step training-accuracy and test-accuracy series for every training fraction; the data-size trend is reported partly as a figure and in summary.
Does not identify Fourier circuits or measure memorizing circuit components being removed. It tests timing of complexity and other candidate transition signals.
Tests weight-norm constraints on modular addition, not initialization-scale changes or grokking on non-algorithmic images, text, or molecules; it does not establish a lazy-to-rich transition.
No realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
Does not test whether a low-norm or circuit-efficiency bias explains grokking. The complexity-controller data boundary is a different mechanism.
Does not compare the learned algorithms across runs, architectures, or hyperparameters for algorithmic identity.
Does not control adaptive-optimizer instabilities or softmax floating-point limits as a test of whether they cause grokking.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU MLP
rows.operation_detail: Change point in map complexity compared with held-out grok step
rows.measure: Median change-point lag to grok; Spearman correlation with seed-specific grok timing
rows.value: KsF change-point median lag 0 steps [−1,500–0]; ρ = 0.872; permutation p = 7 × 10−4; FDR q = 0.0014
rows.note: The signal localizes completion at the transition, rather than showing a lead before it.
rows.check: The change point is defined as the largest one-step change of map complexity. It locates the abrupt function-level collapse at the grok step (lag 0) and cannot show whether internal progress was gradual beforehand. No circuit is measured.

rows.note: BDM localizes completion to about one evaluation interval after the grok step, not before it.
rows.check: Same largest-change-point measure on BDM (lag 250). It localizes completion; it cannot test gradual formation or anticipation.

relationships.condition: Plain full-batch AdamW training of a 2-layer MLP on modular addition and multiplication, p=31
relationships.reason: The plain baselines grok late and the delay shortens with more data (R3, R4). Per the text (Table 5), train fit precedes the grok by a median of about 18,250 steps; that result has no row.
relationships.display_finding: Generalization followed training fit by a median of about 18,250 steps, with shorter delays as training data increased.

relation.reason: The study reports delayed generalization in plain baselines and explicitly tests the training-data dependence of that delay.

tranche.reason: The complexity-controller experiments include plain-training comparisons and diagnostics that directly test grokking and its dependence on training fraction.

source_check.notes: Figure 3 uses three seeds per point and reports grok times conditional on success within 30,000 steps. Grokking is operationally defined as held-out accuracy exceeding 0.9; the rows correctly avoid assigning exact values to unlabeled plotted points.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Plain training and complexity-kicked training on tested modular-arithmetic tasks
reader_labels.reason: The paper describes a shorter grok delay with more training data in both plain baselines, and reports delayed grokking with substantial reductions in steps under the kick in addition runs (R1–R6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Complexity-kicked modular multiplication at 50–60% training data
reader_labels.reason: The kick is less reliable at 50% and slower than plain training at 60%, so its acceleration is not general across tasks (R7–R8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Transition timing signals on modular addition
reader_labels.reason: Map complexity and BDM mark grokking at or near the transition rather than clearly before it; earlier geometric signals are not identified as circuit formation, and representation-tail timing is not significant (R9–R12).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Weak weight decay 0.01 with the ρ=0.3 norm constraint on modular addition
reader_labels.reason: A norm constraint changes outcomes relative to the no-constraint condition, with 2/3 seeds reaching the grok criterion at ρ=0.3 (R17–R18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Other tested norm radii and strong-decay regime
reader_labels.reason: The effect is narrow: other weak-decay radii do not grok, strong-decay runs are characterized as neutral, and releasing the ρ=0.3 constraint reduces final accuracy (R13–R16, R19–R20, R22–R25).
